extracted.intended_audience: public administrators, administrative analysts, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying rational management techniques to public administration, covering political, legal, socio-psychological, and organizational considerations for administrators and administrative analysts. Emphasizes democratic management, legislative interaction, and human factors in implementing procedural reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider political consequences alongside economy and efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: The administrator cannot always follow objective and reasonable considerations of economy and efficiency; he has to consider the political consequences of events which in themselves may be relatively harmless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: elaborate precautions to prevent petty graft are maintained not solely because of the cost of loss but because of political repercussions. Administrators must weigh political fallout when deciding procedures and safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen to both administrative analysts and political advisors
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary for the administrator to listen not only to the administrative analyst, who is concerned mainly with getting work done as efficiently as possible, but also to political advisors who 'keep an ear to the ground' and who study the reactions and behavior of people with whom the organization deals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect tension: political advice may lead to departures from good management or adoption of purposely cumbersome procedures. Balance technical efficiency with political realities (example: insulating field staff by referring applications to a superior office).

rubrics_metrics.name: Precisely define functions and align responsibility with authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A basic rule of good management is that each function and activity should be precisely defined and allocated, and that responsibility and authority should run parallel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This policy should be followed for internal administration, though exceptions may be made under political pressure. Clear allocation reduces confusion and protects against arbitrary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use bureaucratic procedural defences prudently ('run-around')
rubrics_metrics.description: When seekers after special privilege become too insistent, it may be necessary to find ways of 'giving them the run-around.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'weapon of bureaucratic defense' can shield the organization from flank attacks but can be abused to cover up error and indolence; use sparingly and with safeguards to prevent misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish legitimate from illegitimate political pressure, recognizing ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: The administrator is expected to distinguish between legitimate and illegitimate politics — respond sympathetically to 'proper' requests and refuse 'improper' demands — but the distinction is not clear and depends on the prevailing political ethos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that the same actors may produce proposals labeled proper or improper by different partisans; judgments should be made in context of community norms rather than moralizing alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure political objectives permit rational management and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Rational management technique, which depends on criticism of methods, discussion of objectives, and free interchange of information, is possible only when political objectives can be analyzed without fear of embarrassment and operations contain nothing to be hidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If political aims require secrecy or concealment, rational technique will be difficult to implement; strive for transparency consistent with legitimate confidentiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislation should set objectives and leave details to administrators
rubrics_metrics.description: A distinction can be drawn between functions of legislation — establishment of objectives and broad programs — and the function of administrative planning — precise definition of purpose and arrangement of ways and means; legislation should eschew detail, stating desired results and leaving how to administrators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice enabling legislation often goes into detail; administrators should advocate for laws that permit flexible execution and interpretation to serve desired ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for enabling legislation that unnecessarily compels administrators
rubrics_metrics.description: As a matter of practice, enabling legislation goes into detail more often than not and sets forth specific ways and means which administrators are compelled to utilize; if details do not work out, administration may be hamstrung.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrators will try to influence legislation; absolute bans on legislative activity by civil servants are nearly impossible and often unwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislators should consider administrative processes and constructive interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislators would simplify administration by keeping in mind (1) the administrative processes necessary for executing laws and (2) the constructive interpretation of laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend review and periodic simplification of enacted laws by their sponsors to reduce administrative burdens; design laws with administration in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of judicial and accounting interpretations that add constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The administrator must reckon with restrictive interpretations laid down by courts and the Comptroller General (e.g., the narrow reading of 'public exigency' and bid solicitation requirements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand how interpretations can add procedural layers (e.g., freight rate computations); use statistical analysis and administrative experience to argue for practical thresholds (example: weight thresholds for freight rate computations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate that legislative control may ossify procedures; design countermeasures
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress tends to enact detailed laws to retain control; legislative control can unintentionally hamstring administration and ossify procedures that should be flexible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design control mechanisms that both check the executive and facilitate streamlining, such as means of transmitting information and making constructive criticism in both directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create institutional legislative support for administrative simplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose a permanent Joint Committee on Administrative Management to consider organization, procedure, and business management of Government offices and to review pending laws with a view to making them as simple to administer as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a committee should have a permanent staff of experts to investigate proposals, advise on feasibility, prepare necessary legislation, and cooperate with other committees; it would provide Congress independent administrative technical capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study administrative phases of new laws before enactment and revise legal structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Rationalization and simplification of administration can progress only so far without corresponding changes in its legal environment; it is important to develop means of studying administrative phases of new laws before enactment and of gradually revising the present legal structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build review processes into legislative drafting and post-enactment oversight to detect and correct administrability problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize socio-psychological resistance to change
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative procedure is a pattern of human behavior and hard to change; resistance to change is a deep-seated instinct rooted in fear of job loss, dislike of strange situations, and desire to entrench position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid blunt orders when possible; seek to get subordinates to work with reforms rather than merely under authority. Anticipate panic, rumors, and defensive reactions that can disorganize work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect workload data sensitively to avoid defensive reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: The administrative analyst may be hampered in securing workload data because operating units may become defensive, dig up reasons for current practices, or withhold information fearing reductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach data collection with tact; show falsity of prejudice against scientific management; emphasize benefits and avoid implying blame to reduce obstructionism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share benefits of efficiency and maintain ethical management
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific management has a code of ethics: the benefits of efficiency should be shared by all concerned — the entrepreneur, the worker, and the public; methods perverted for anti-social ends are abuses, not scientific management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote social consciousness in management reforms; counter stereotypes of the 'efficiency man' as a job-cutter by demonstrating shared gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage staff reductions humanely and avoid direct link between abolition and dismissal
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever improved operation releases employees, savings can be used for new positions; when reductions are unavoidable, sever the connection between abolition of a job and discharge of its incumbent even at some cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reserve pools, training, and organization-wide separation registers based on objective information; avoid dismissing those whose particular jobs are terminated as the line of least resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make management democratic and inclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative management must be thoroughly democratic: not a mystery propounded by a caste of intellectual priests, but a common way of doing things accepted by everybody; the analyst should learn from executives, supervisors, operators, and clerks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop capacity for listening and understanding; speak the common language; sell ideas in terms of operating people's experience; encourage wide participation in shaping plans to ease implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat administrative analysis as collaborative, not proprietary
rubrics_metrics.description: The administrative analyst must work with people and accept that few worthwhile results will be exclusively his own; final plans are usually a synthesis of ideas gathered from operating officials plus those of the analyst which stand up under criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist exploiting exclusive knowledge; act as leader and coordinator rather than manipulator; discount obstructionism but seek broad participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote two-way planning and educate employees in objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: New trends call for 'two-way planning' — from the bottom up as well as from the top down; examples include project work budgets and job load analysis, and programs that enlist collaboration of customers and field staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educate all employees in objectives and philosophy before implementing work simplification; reorganize operations with input from those who do the jobs rather than imposing systems from outside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diffuse administrative knowledge to enable sustained progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific management and rational technique are products not only of specialized knowledge but of the diffusion of that knowledge among those whom it affects; only as the natural laws and human equations of administration are assimilated by all participants is sustained progress possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in spreading understanding of administrative principles and techniques across the organization so improvements are owned and sustained by participants.
